mcqs.learning_point: Understand field around a circular loop
mcqs.question: A circular loop of radius 5 cm carries a current of 2 A in the clockwise direction when viewed from above. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop?
mcqs.explanation: Using the right‑hand thumb rule for a current loop, curl the fingers in the direction of the current (clockwise as seen). The thumb then points into the page, indicating the magnetic field direction at the centre. Options B, C and D do not follow this rule.

mcqs.question: A small compass is placed 3 cm to the right of a long straight wire carrying a current upward. The compass needle turns and points downward. What does this observation tell about the magnetic field produced by the wire at that point?

options.A: The magnetic field is radial outward from the wire
options.B: The magnetic field forms concentric circles around the wire
options.C: The magnetic field is uniform and vertical

mcqs.answer: The magnetic field forms concentric circles around the wire
mcqs.explanation: A current‑carrying straight conductor creates a magnetic field that circles the wire (right‑hand rule). The downward deflection of the compass needle shows the field direction is tangential to a circular line around the wire. Options A, C and D are inconsistent with the observed behavior.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about magnetic field lines around a current‑carrying straight conductor is correct?

options.A: Magnetic field lines start from the conductor and end at infinity
options.B: Magnetic field lines are straight lines parallel to the wire
options.C: Magnetic field lines form closed concentric circles around the wire
options.D: Magnetic field lines go from north to south poles only

mcqs.answer: Magnetic field lines form closed concentric circles around the wire
mcqs.explanation: The magnetic field produced by a straight conductor is represented by closed circular lines centred on the wire. They do not start or end anywhere (ruling out A), are not straight (ruling out B), and the north‑south pole description applies to permanent magnets, not to fields around conductors (ruling out D).

mcqs.learning_point: Understand field around a straight conductor
mcqs.question: If the magnetic field strength at a point P located 2 cm from a long straight wire is B1, what will be the magnetic field strength at a point Q located 6 cm from the same wire (same current)? Assume the medium is air.
mcqs.explanation: For a straight conductor, magnetic field magnitude B = μ0 I / (2πr), so B is inversely proportional to the distance r. Increasing the distance from 2 cm to 6 cm triples r, therefore the field becomes one‑third of its original value. Options B, C and D do not follow the 1/r relationship.

mcqs.question: How does the right‑hand thumb rule differ when applied to (i) a straight current‑carrying conductor and (ii) a solenoid?

options.A: In both cases the thumb points in the direction of the magnetic field inside the object
options.B: For the straight conductor the thumb gives the direction of current while the curled fingers give the field direction; for the solenoid the thumb gives the direction of the magnetic field inside the coil
options.C: The rule is identical for both; thumb always indicates the direction of current
options.D: The rule cannot be applied to a solenoid

mcqs.answer: For the straight conductor the thumb gives the direction of current while the curled fingers give the field direction; for the solenoid the thumb gives the direction of the magnetic field inside the coil
mcqs.explanation: In a straight wire, the right‑hand thumb points along the current and the fingers wrap to show the circular magnetic field. In a solenoid, the thumb points along the axis of the coil indicating the direction of the magnetic field inside, while the fingers curl in the direction of the current flowing through the windings. Options A, C and D misstate the application of the rule.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand field around a circular loop
mcqs.question: A circular loop of radius 10 cm carries a current of 5 A. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop? (μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
mcqs.explanation: For a single circular loop, B = μ0 I / (2R). Substituting μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷, I = 5 A, R = 0.10 m gives B = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 5) / (2 × 0.10) = (20π×10⁻⁷) / 0.20 = 100π×10⁻⁷ = π×10⁻⁵ ≈ 3.14×10⁻⁵ T. Option A matches this calculation; the other options are multiples or fractions of the correct value.

mcqs.question: Which statement best defines a magnetic field?

options.A: A region where magnetic forces can act on moving charges or magnetic materials
options.B: A force that pulls two magnets together
options.C: The flow of electric current in a wire
options.D: The electric field produced by a charged particle

mcqs.answer: A region where magnetic forces can act on moving charges or magnetic materials
mcqs.explanation: A magnetic field is a vector field that exerts forces on moving electric charges (via the Lorentz force) and on magnetic dipoles. Option B describes a consequence, not the definition; C describes electric current; D describes an electric field, not magnetic.

mcqs.question: How are magnetic field lines around a long straight current‑carrying conductor correctly represented?

options.A: Straight lines parallel to the wire
options.B: Concentric circles centered on the wire

mcqs.answer: Concentric circles centered on the wire
mcqs.explanation: The magnetic field produced by a straight conductor forms closed circular loops around the wire, as shown by the right‑hand rule. Straight, radial, or random lines do not represent the actual field geometry.
